beliefs.practice: Read the DocumentDB connection string (DOCUMENTDB_URI) from an environment variable at runtime and never commit it to source control or log it; provide a .env.example with a placeholder instead.
Use a single, long-lived async client/connection pool per process (do not create a new client per request); initialize the Beanie/Motor client at application startup and reuse it for all requests.
Enable and use TLS/SSL for connections to the DocumentDB endpoint; verify certificates where possible instead of disabling verification in production.
Store secrets (API keys, DB credentials) in a secrets manager (Azure Key Vault) for production and load them into the app at runtime rather than embedding in code or config files.

Use principle of least privilege for DB credentials: create a DB user with only the specific database and collection privileges needed (read/write on sample_retail_19 collections) rather than using an account with cluster-admin rights.
Model co-purchase pair documents with a deterministic composite id (e.g., sorted product_id pair) to make aggregation idempotent and avoid duplicate pair documents.

Keep vector embeddings as a fixed-length numeric array field (floats) and store a separate normalized vector field if you want to compute cosine similarity efficiently without normalizing at query time.

Create appropriate indexes: a 1) compound index on pair identifiers and co-purchase count for fast lookup/sorting, and 2) a vector index (specifying index type like HNSW/IVF/DiskANN and appropriate params such as M/efConstruction or nlist/ef) on the vector field for nearest-neighbor search.

When creating a vector index, set index parameters to trade off recall vs latency appropriate for the workload (e.g., HNSW: set M and efConstruction during index build; use efSearch/ef during query time), and test recall on sample queries.

For ranking combine signals deterministically: compute cosine similarity on normalized vectors and combine with a scaled co-purchase count (e.g., affinity = alpha * cosine + beta * log(count+1)) rather than adding raw counts to the similarity score.
Normalize vectors at write-time (store unit-length vectors) so similarity queries can use dot-product for cosine and avoid normalizing each candidate during query.
Use batched upserts when seeding/refreshing pair documents (bulk write with upsert) to make the seed script idempotent and reduce round-trips.

Implement retries with exponential backoff and jitter for transient network or throughput errors, and treat 429/TooManyRequests and network timeouts as retryable; however, cap retries to avoid overwhelming the service.

Instrument and monitor query latency and index usage: capture slow queries and vector search latencies; enable server-side logging/metrics where provided and emit app-level metrics (histograms) for the /cross-sell endpoint.
Limit returned fields in queries (projection) to only what the endpoint needs (e.g., product_id, affinity, metadata) and avoid returning large embedding vectors in the response unless required.

When performing vector nearest-neighbor queries, use an appropriate candidate fetch size (k) larger than the desired top-N and then rerank in-app using the full affinity formula rather than trusting the DB to perfectly rank the final metric if the DB only indexes by vector similarity.
Set sensible timeouts for external calls (embedding API calls) and DB operations; make seed and batch jobs tolerant to partial failures and allow resume/rollback by idempotent keys.

Use typed ODM models (Beanie/Pydantic) with explicit schemas, field types and validation for vectors (list[float] of fixed length) so bad embeddings or malformed pair documents are rejected before insertion.

Avoid large unbounded transactions: update pair counts with atomic single-document updates (increments) or bulk operations; don’t attempt cross-collection multi-document transactions at scale for aggregation updates.

Run index creation and reindexing as an idempotent, offline/maintenance step (not during regular request processing) and verify index status via the cluster tooling before relying on them for production queries.
